republic-of-venice.t: The 'Most Serene Republic', a merchant state on the lagoon that ruled a maritime empire across the Adriatic and Aegean for a thousand years until Napoleon ended it in 1797.
republic-of-venice.o: Refugees from mainland cities settled the lagoon islands during the barbarian invasions. Venetian tradition places the election of the first doge, Paolo Lucio Anafesto, in 697, under Byzantine overlordship. After resisting Pepin of Italy in 810 the government moved to the Rialto islands, and in 828 merchants brought the relics of Saint Mark, the city's patron.
republic-of-venice.r: Venice was an aristocratic republic headed by an elected doge for life, whose power was increasingly checked by councils. The 1297 'Serrata' closed the Great Council to a hereditary nobility, and the Council of Ten guarded security. Trade privileges in Byzantium from 1082 and the Fourth Crusade of 1204, led by Doge Enrico Dandolo, built a Stato da Mar of Dalmatia, Crete, Corfu and later Cyprus. The Arsenal, glass-making and printing made it an industrial and cultural centre.
republic-of-venice.e: Wars with the Ottomans cost Venice Cyprus (1571), Crete (1669) and the Morea (1718). In 1797 Napoleon forced the last doge, Ludovico Manin, to abdicate, and the Treaty of Campo Formio handed Venice to Austria. It joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.

republic-of-the-seven-tenths.t: Alpine peasant republic of the upper Rhône valley, an ally of the Swiss Confederacy that ruled itself through seven communal districts.
republic-of-the-seven-tenths.o: The communities (Zenden) of the Upper Valais had long contested power with the prince-bishop of Sion. After decades of struggle, the Zenden forced Bishop Hildebrand Jost to abandon most of his temporal rights in 1628 and finally in 1634, and the Valais became a republic of seven tenths: Goms, Brig, Visp, Raron, Leuk, Sierre and Sion.
republic-of-the-seven-tenths.r: Sovereignty lay with the Diet (Landrat), in which each tenth sent delegates, while the bishop kept a largely honorary role. The republic was a Zugewandter Ort, an associate of the Old Swiss Confederacy, and governed the French-speaking Lower Valais as a subject territory. Its economy rested on Alpine farming and trade over the Simplon pass, dominated by families such as the Stockalper of Brig.
republic-of-the-seven-tenths.e: The Lower Valais rebelled in 1798 and French troops entered the country. Valais was incorporated into the Helvetic Republic in 1798, later becoming the Rhodanic Republic, a French department, and in 1815 a Swiss canton.

restoration-spain.t: The restored Bourbon monarchy of Alfonso XII and Alfonso XIII, a stable but rigged parliamentary system that lost Spain's last colonies in 1898.
restoration-spain.o: In December 1874 General Arsenio Martínez Campos proclaimed Alfonso XII, son of Isabella II, at Sagunto, ending the Sexenio Democrático. The conservative statesman Antonio Cánovas del Castillo designed the new order and its Constitution of 1876.
restoration-spain.r: Under the turno pacífico, Cánovas's Conservatives and Sagasta's Liberals alternated in power through elections managed by local bosses, the caciques. The system kept order but excluded workers and regionalists. Defeat by the United States in 1898 cost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines, and the Tragic Week of 1909 and the disaster of Annual in Morocco in 1921 shook the regime.
restoration-spain.e: Alfonso XIII backed Miguel Primo de Rivera's dictatorship from 1923 to 1930. After republican victories in the municipal elections of April 1931, the king left Spain, and the Second Spanish Republic was proclaimed.

remi.t: Belgic people of Champagne who sided with Caesar from the start, making Reims the chief Roman city of northern Gaul.
remi.o: The Remi held the chalk plains of Champagne around Durocortorum (Reims). In 57 BCE, while the other Belgae formed a league against Rome, they sent the envoys Iccius and Andecomborius to offer Caesar their submission and support.
remi.r: They shared laws and magistrates with their kinsmen the Suessiones and controlled a network of oppida. Their loyalty brought them supremacy over neighbouring peoples, and Caesar used their land as a base throughout his campaigns.
remi.e: Under Rome Durocortorum became capital of the province of Gallia Belgica, with monuments such as the Porte de Mars. As Reims it became an archbishopric, where Bishop Remigius baptised Clovis of the Kingdom of the Franks and French kings were later crowned.

rueda-de-jalon-hudid.t: The last refuge of the Hudid kings of Zaragoza, a castle state on the Jalón kept alive through alliance with the Christian kings.
rueda-de-jalon-hudid.o: When the Almoravids took Zaragoza in 1110, the Hudid heir Abd al-Malik Imad al-Dawla withdrew to the strong castle of Rueda de Jalón, west of the city, and continued to rule a small territory from there, relying on Alfonso I of Aragon against the Almoravids.
rueda-de-jalon-hudid.r: The Hudid remnant was a client principality, surviving between Almoravid Zaragoza and the advancing Kingdom of Aragon. After Abd al-Malik's death in 1130 his son Ahmad Sayf al-Dawla, known to Christians as Zafadola, negotiated with Alfonso VII of Castile.
rueda-de-jalon-hudid.e: Zafadola handed Rueda to Alfonso VII in exchange for lands near Toledo and became a Castilian vassal. He later led Andalusi revolts against the Almoravids and was killed in 1146. The castle passed to Aragon.

republic-of-mulhouse.t: A Protestant city-republic in Alsace allied to the Swiss, which grew rich on printed cotton and chose to join France in 1798.
republic-of-mulhouse.o: Mulhouse was an imperial town in Upper Alsace that gradually freed itself from local lords and, by the mid-14th century, governed itself through a council and mayor under the emperor. In 1354 it joined the Décapole, the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
republic-of-mulhouse.r: Threatened by the Habsburgs, Mulhouse allied with Basel and the Swiss cantons, becoming an associate of the Swiss Confederation in 1515 and leaving the Décapole. It adopted the Reformed faith in the 1520s. From 1746 its merchants founded calico-printing works, making printed cotton, the indiennes, the basis of a major textile industry.
republic-of-mulhouse.e: Surrounded by French territory and strangled by customs barriers after the Revolution, the citizens voted in January 1798 to join the French First Republic. Mulhouse became a leading French industrial city.

republic-of-poljica.t: Self-governing peasant and minor-noble community between Split and Omiš that kept its own law and elected rulers for nearly four centuries.
republic-of-poljica.o: Poljica, a hilly district between the Cetina river and the coast near Split, had long enjoyed local autonomy under Croatian and Hungarian kings. Its customary law was written down in the Poljica Statute, traditionally dated to 1440, which fixed the rights of its villages and noble families. As the Ottomans advanced, Poljica placed itself under Venetian protection.
republic-of-poljica.r: Each year an assembly at Gata elected a grand knez from the local nobility, assisted by village knezes, judges and a chancellor. Land was held by kin groups, and the statute regulated inheritance, feuds and grazing. The statute was written in Croatian in Bosnian Cyrillic script. Poljica paid tribute to the Ottomans while serving Venice as a frontier buffer.
republic-of-poljica.e: After Venice fell in 1797, Poljica came under Austria and then, in 1806, France. When Poljica men joined a Russian-backed rising, Marshal Marmont abolished the republic in 1807 and merged it into French Dalmatia, later the Illyrian Provinces. The statute remains a key source for Croatian law.

rhegion.t: Greek city on the toe of Italy guarding the Strait of Messina, which under the tyrant Anaxilas controlled both shores of the strait.
rhegion.o: Chalcidians from Euboea, joined by exiles from Messenia, founded Rhegion around 720 BCE at the southern tip of Calabria, on the Delphic oracle's advice according to tradition. Facing Zancle across the Strait, it controlled shipping between the Tyrrhenian and Ionian Seas.
rhegion.r: Rhegion adopted the laws of Charondas and was ruled by an aristocracy of Messenian descent until Anaxilas made himself tyrant around 494 BCE. He seized Zancle, renamed it Messana, and allied with Carthage. The city was later a democracy and an ally of Athens. The lyric poet Ibycus and the sculptor Pythagoras came from Rhegion. Its coins showing a lion's head and a hare are well known.
rhegion.e: Dionysius I captured and destroyed Rhegion in 387 BCE, but it revived. In 280 BCE, during the war with Pyrrhus, a Roman garrison of Campanian troops seized the city; Rome retook it in 270 BCE and executed the mutineers. It remained a Greek-speaking ally, later Rhegium Iulium, and is today Reggio Calabria.

republic-of-ancona.t: Self-governing Adriatic port and maritime republic that traded with Dalmatia and the Levant until the papacy took full control in 1532.
republic-of-ancona.o: Ancona, a port founded by Greeks from Syracuse in about 387 BCE, kept trading links across the Adriatic through the early Middle Ages. Around the start of the 11th century it began governing itself as a commune within the March of Ancona, under loose papal and imperial overlordship.
republic-of-ancona.r: Ancona was ruled by elected consuls, later by a council of elders, and was a merchant republic with trading houses in Constantinople, Alexandria and the Dalmatian ports, often allied with Ragusa against Venice. It famously resisted Frederick Barbarossa's siege in 1173 with Byzantine support; the widow Stamura became a local heroine. Its maritime statutes regulated Adriatic trade.
republic-of-ancona.e: In 1532 Pope Clement VII brought Ancona under direct papal rule, installing a garrison and building a fortress. The city remained the main port of the Papal States until it joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1860.

republic-of-alsace-lorraine.t: A short-lived republic declared in Strasbourg as German rule collapsed in November 1918, swept away when French troops arrived days later.
republic-of-alsace-lorraine.o: As the German Empire collapsed in November 1918, soldiers' and workers' councils formed in Strasbourg and other towns of the Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine. On 11 November the regional parliament constituted itself as a national council, and a republic was declared amid competing plans for autonomy.
republic-of-alsace-lorraine.r: Power was divided between the soldiers' councils, some influenced by revolutionary socialism, and the national council and Strasbourg's socialist mayor, Jacques Peirotes. The new authorities tried to keep order as German troops withdrew, but the republic had no recognition or real administration.
republic-of-alsace-lorraine.e: French troops entered Strasbourg on 22 November 1918 and the councils dissolved. The Treaty of Versailles confirmed the return of Alsace-Lorraine to France.

republic-of-ossola.t: The best-known partisan republic of wartime Italy, which governed the Alpine valleys around Domodossola for about forty days in 1944.
republic-of-ossola.o: In September 1944 Italian partisan formations drove German and Fascist garrisons out of the Val d'Ossola, near the Swiss border, and entered Domodossola on 10 September. A provisional government junta was formed, presided over by the socialist Ettore Tibaldi.
republic-of-ossola.r: The junta brought together members of the different anti-Fascist parties. In a few weeks it reorganised local government, schools, justice and food supply, and planned democratic reforms, while the Swiss border allowed contacts with the Allies. Its experience of self-government later influenced debates on the Italian constitution.
republic-of-ossola.e: In October 1944 German and Fascist troops of the Italian Social Republic launched an offensive and reoccupied the valley. Thousands of civilians and partisans fled into Switzerland.

rusellae.t: Etruscan hill city near modern Grosseto, ringed by massive walls, which overlooked the Lake Prile lagoon until Rome captured it in 294 BCE.
rusellae.o: Rusellae, modern Roselle, occupied two hills above the coastal plain of the Ombrone, then bordering the lagoon of Lake Prile. Settled from the Villanovan period, it grew into a city in the 7th century BCE, when houses of unbaked brick were built, and in the 6th century it was enclosed by walls of huge polygonal blocks some 3 km long.
rusellae.r: Its prosperity came from farming the Ombrone plain, fishing and salt in the lagoon, and links with the mining districts of Vetulonia, which it overtook in importance during the 6th century BCE. Excavation has revealed a forum area, houses and craft quarters, but little is known of its government beyond the general Etruscan pattern of aristocratic magistrates.
rusellae.e: Livy records that Lucius Postumius Megellus stormed Rusellae in 294 BCE, taking 2,000 prisoners. As a Roman ally it sent grain and timber for Scipio's fleet in 205 BCE, and later became a Roman colony with a forum, baths and amphitheatre. It remained a bishopric until the see moved to Grosseto in 1138.

republic-of-marseille.t: A brief maritime commune in which the merchants of Marseille governed their port independently before Charles of Anjou crushed it.
republic-of-marseille.o: In the early 13th century the citizens of the lower town of Marseille bought out the rights of their viscounts and formed a commune, organised around the Confraternity of the Holy Spirit. The register dates the republic from 1214, while the upper town remained under the bishop.
republic-of-marseille.r: The commune elected a podestà on the Italian model and a council of citizens, issued statutes and ran its own trade with the Levant, Sicily and North Africa, rivalling Genoa and Pisa. It joined the opposition to the counts of Provence and backed Raymond VII of Toulouse.
republic-of-marseille.e: Charles of Anjou, the new count of Provence, forced the city to submit in 1252 and, after further revolts, imposed the Chapters of Peace in 1257, ending its independence. Marseille kept municipal privileges within the County of Provence.

republic-of-florence.t: The city-republic of bankers and wool merchants that minted the florin and nurtured Dante, Giotto, Brunelleschi and the Medici-led Renaissance.
republic-of-florence.o: After Matilda of Canossa died in 1115, Florence's citizens took control of the city, and consuls are recorded by the 1130s. The commune conquered its rural territory, destroyed nearby Fiesole in 1125 and became the strongest power in Tuscany during the 13th century.
republic-of-florence.r: Florence was ruled by priors elected from the guilds, under the Ordinances of Justice of 1293 that excluded magnates. The gold florin, first minted in 1252, became Europe's standard coin, and banks such as the Bardi, Peruzzi and Medici lent across Europe. Guelph-Ghibelline and Black-White feuds exiled Dante. From 1434 Cosimo de' Medici and his grandson Lorenzo steered the republic informally while patronising Renaissance art and learning.
republic-of-florence.e: The Medici were expelled in 1494; Savonarola and then Piero Soderini led the restored republic until the Medici returned in 1512. A last republic fell after the siege of 1529–1530, and in 1532 Alessandro de' Medici became duke, creating the Duchy of Florence.

redones.t: Gallic people of eastern Brittany whose chief town Condate became the city of Rennes.
redones.o: The Redones lived in the basin of the Vilaine, in the modern Ille-et-Vilaine. Caesar lists them among the Armorican peoples who submitted to Publius Crassus in 57 BCE.
redones.r: Their oppidum of Condate stood at the confluence of the Ille and the Vilaine, as its Gaulish name, meaning confluence, indicates. They struck gold coins of Armorican type.
redones.e: They sent troops to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE. Under Rome Condate became a walled civitas capital, called Redones in late antiquity, the origin of Rennes, later the capital of the Duchy of Brittany.

raurici.t: Celtic people of the Rhine bend around Basel who joined the Helvetii's failed migration and later saw Rome found Augusta Raurica.
raurici.o: The Raurici lived along the upper Rhine around the Basel region and in the southern Alsace and Jura. Caesar records them as neighbours and allies of the Helvetii.
raurici.r: Their oppidum on the Münsterhügel in Basel and the earlier open settlement at Basel-Gasfabrik show a wealthy community trading on the Rhine.
raurici.e: In 58 BCE they burned their homes and joined the migration of the Helvetii, but after the defeat at Bibracte they were sent back. Around 44 BCE Lucius Munatius Plancus founded the colony of Augusta Raurica (Augst) in their land.

roman-republic.t: The Roman state from the expulsion of the kings to Augustus, which grew from a city in Latium to master of the Mediterranean before collapsing in civil war.
roman-republic.o: Tradition dates the Republic to 509 BCE, when Roman aristocrats expelled Tarquinius Superbus and replaced the king with two consuls elected each year. The early Republic was a small city-state in Latium, at war with its neighbours and divided internally between patricians and plebeians.
roman-republic.r: Power was shared between annual magistrates, the Senate of former officials and the citizen assemblies, with tribunes protecting plebeians. The Twelve Tables of 451–450 BCE codified law. Rome conquered Italy by 270 BCE through alliances and colonies, defeated Carthage in the Punic Wars, and took Macedon, Greece, Spain and Africa. Conquest brought slaves, wealth and an army of professional soldiers loyal to their generals, while Greek culture transformed Roman literature and art.
roman-republic.e: From the Gracchi in 133 BCE, political violence grew: Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Julius Caesar fought civil wars, and Caesar became dictator for life before his murder in 44 BCE. After Octavian defeated Antony at Actium in 31 BCE he received the name Augustus in 27 BCE, beginning the Roman Empire.

republic-of-noli.t: A tiny Ligurian seaside republic that kept its independence, under Genoese protection, from 1192 until 1797.
republic-of-noli.o: Noli, a small port on the western Riviera, freed itself from the Del Carretto marquises and became a self-governing commune in 1192. It soon placed itself under the protection of the Republic of Genoa while keeping its own institutions.
republic-of-noli.r: Noli was governed by consuls and later by a council and podestà, and lived from fishing, shipbuilding and sea trade. Its ships joined Genoese expeditions, including crusading voyages. In 1239 Pope Gregory IX made it a bishopric, a sign of its standing. The town kept its medieval walls, towers and the Romanesque church of San Paragorio.
republic-of-noli.e: Noli survived as a nominal republic allied to Genoa for six centuries. It was absorbed into the French-backed Ligurian Republic in 1797.

republic-of-san-marco.t: The revolutionary Venetian republic of 1848–1849 led by Daniele Manin, which held out against an Austrian siege for seventeen months.
republic-of-san-marco.o: On 22 March 1848, as revolution spread across Europe, the Venetians rose against the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia, freed the lawyer Daniele Manin from prison and took the Arsenal. Manin proclaimed the Republic of San Marco, reviving the name of the old Republic of Venice.
republic-of-san-marco.r: Manin led the government, with the writer Niccolò Tommaseo among its ministers. The republic briefly voted in July 1848 to join the Kingdom of Sardinia, but after Piedmont's defeat at Custoza it returned to independence. Venetians raised loans, printed paper money and organised a national guard and defence of the lagoon, which became a symbol of Italian resistance.
republic-of-san-marco.e: Austrian forces besieged Venice from 1849, bombarding the city while cholera and hunger spread. The republic surrendered in August 1849, and Manin went into exile in Paris. Venetia joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.

republic-of-amalfi.t: Maritime republic on the Sorrento peninsula whose merchants traded with Constantinople, Egypt and Jerusalem in the 10th and 11th centuries.
republic-of-amalfi.o: Amalfi was a small fortified town on the steep coast of the Sorrento peninsula, part of the Byzantine Duchy of Naples. In 839, after the Lombard prince Sicard of Benevento had attacked it and taken its people away, the Amalfitans broke from Naples and elected their own leaders, first prefects and later judges.
republic-of-amalfi.r: From 958 Amalfi was ruled by dukes, among them Manso I, who also controlled Salerno. With little farmland, it lived from trade: its merchants had colonies in Constantinople, Antioch and Cairo and founded a hospital in Jerusalem from which the Knights Hospitaller later emerged. It minted gold tari, and the maritime code known as the Tabula Amalphitana was used across the Mediterranean.
republic-of-amalfi.e: Robert Guiscard took Amalfi in 1073. It revolted and was absorbed by Roger II's Kingdom of Sicily in 1131. Pisa sacked it in 1135 and 1137, and a storm in 1343 destroyed much of the lower town. Its cathedral and the Amalfi Coast are now famous.

rhodes.t: Island republic created in 408 BCE that became the leading Hellenistic naval and commercial power of the eastern Mediterranean, home of the Colossus.
rhodes.o: The three old Dorian cities of the island, Ialysos, Kamiros and Lindos, joined in 408-407 BCE to found a single new city of Rhodes at the island's northern tip. Laid out on a regular grid with fine harbours, it quickly drew population and trade, while the old towns survived as districts of the unified state.
rhodes.r: Rhodes was governed by an assembly, council and annual prytaneis, with a moderate democracy that favoured its wealthy shipowners. It lived by trade in grain and wine, policed the sea against pirates, and its maritime law influenced later Roman law. Withstanding the siege of Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305-304 BCE, it built the Colossus. Its schools of rhetoric and philosophy attracted Romans.
rhodes.e: Siding with Rome against Philip V and Antiochus III won Rhodes lands in Caria and Lycia, but Rome punished its wavering by making Delos a free port in 167 BCE. Cassius sacked it in 43 BCE. Claudius withdrew its freedom in 44 CE, and it was later absorbed into the province of Asia.

roman-republic-1798-1799.t: A French-sponsored republic proclaimed in Rome in 1798 after Pope Pius VI was deposed and sent into exile.
roman-republic-1798-1799.o: After the French general Duphot was killed in a riot in Rome in December 1797, French troops under General Berthier occupied the city. On 15 February 1798 a republic was proclaimed in the Forum, ending the temporal power of the Papal States. Pope Pius VI was deported and died in exile at Valence in 1799.
roman-republic-1798-1799.r: The republic adopted a constitution modelled on the French Directory but using ancient Roman titles, with consuls, a senate and a tribunate. It absorbed the Anconine Republic and the Tiberina Republic. French commissioners controlled it, heavy levies and confiscations of art and church property caused hardship, and peasant revolts broke out.
roman-republic-1798-1799.e: In November 1798 the Kingdom of Naples briefly occupied Rome. As the French retreated from Italy in 1799, Neapolitan troops ended the republic in September, and the papacy was restored under Pius VII.

robogdii.t: People of the north coast of Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, near a headland he called Robogdium, probably in County Antrim.
robogdii.o: The Robogdii are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them on the north coast of Ireland. A nearby headland, Robogdium Promontorium, is usually identified with Fair Head or a neighbouring point in north Antrim, facing Kintyre across the North Channel.
robogdii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. Their coast lay only a short sea crossing from Scotland, a route that in later centuries carried the Dál Riata between Antrim and Argyll, and similar close contact across the channel was probably already important in their time.
robogdii.e: The Robogdii are not mentioned again, and no Irish population name has been securely matched with theirs. North Antrim later formed part of the lands of Dál Riata and the Dal nAraidi.

republic-of-pechina.t: A self-governing community of Andalusi sailors near Almería that traded across the Mediterranean and founded Oran in 902.
republic-of-pechina.o: Around 884 a community of Andalusi seafarers, the bahriyyun, settled at Bajjana (Pechina) in the lower Andarax valley near Almería, with the permission of the emir and alongside local Arab families. They formed a self-governing body during the decline of central authority in al-Andalus.
republic-of-pechina.r: Pechina was run by a council of sailors rather than a single ruler, recognising the emir only nominally. It lived from maritime trade with North Africa, and its sailors founded trading posts on the African coast, including Oran in 902. Almería served as its harbour and watchtower, and the town grew wealthy as a port for the Mediterranean.
republic-of-pechina.e: Abd al-Rahman III brought Pechina under direct control around 922. Its harbour, Almería, then eclipsed it, becoming the main naval base of the Caliphate of Córdoba, and Pechina declined into a village.

republic-of-bergamo.t: A republic proclaimed when Bergamo rose against Venetian rule with French backing in March 1797, before joining the Cisalpine Republic.
republic-of-bergamo.o: Bergamo had been a mainland city of the Republic of Venice since 1428. In March 1797, with French troops in the city, local Jacobins proclaimed Bergamo's independence from Venice and set up a provisional government.
republic-of-bergamo.r: The Bergamasque Republic was a provisional regime of local patriots under French protection. It abolished Venetian institutions, planted liberty trees and sought union with the new republics of Lombardy. Its revolt helped trigger risings in Brescia and Crema, which weakened Venice in the last weeks before its fall.
republic-of-bergamo.e: Venice fell in May 1797, and later that year Bergamo was united to the Cisalpine Republic, created by Napoleon.

republic-of-genoa-1814.t: A brief restoration of the old Genoese republic under British protection in 1814, before the Congress of Vienna gave Genoa to Piedmont.
republic-of-genoa-1814.o: In April 1814 British forces under Lord William Bentinck landed and took Genoa from the French. Bentinck, hoping to rally Italians against Napoleon, proclaimed the restoration of the Republic of Genoa under the old constitution of 1797, with a provisional government led by Girolamo Serra.
republic-of-genoa-1814.r: The provisional government tried to revive the institutions of the old aristocratic republic and lobbied the allied powers for recognition. It controlled Genoa and the Ligurian coast but had no army of its own and relied on British protection.
republic-of-genoa-1814.e: The great powers had already decided to strengthen Piedmont as a barrier against France. The Congress of Vienna gave Genoa to the Kingdom of Sardinia, which took possession in January 1815, despite Genoese protests.

roman-kingdom.t: Rome under its seven kings, traditionally 753–509 BCE, when a Latin settlement on the Tiber became a city with temples, a forum and institutions that outlived the monarchy.
roman-kingdom.o: Rome grew from Iron Age villages on the Palatine and nearby hills by the Tiber crossing. Tradition dated its founding by Romulus to 753 BCE; archaeology shows settlement from the 10th century BCE and the drainage and paving of the Forum around 650–600 BCE, when the villages became a single city.
roman-kingdom.r: The king (rex) ruled with the advice of a Senate of clan elders, and the people were organised in thirty curiae. Tradition credits Numa Pompilius with Rome's religious institutions and Servius Tullius with the census and a new army based on wealth classes. The last three kings had Etruscan links; under them Rome built the Cloaca Maxima and the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, and became the leading city of Latium.
roman-kingdom.e: Tradition says that after Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, Lucius Junius Brutus led the nobles in expelling Tarquinius Superbus in 509 BCE. The kingship was replaced by two annually elected consuls, founding the Roman Republic. The title rex survived only in a priesthood, and Romans long hated the very word.

roman-britain.t: The Roman province of Britannia, ruled from 43 until about 410, which brought towns, roads, villas, Latin and Christianity to most of what is now England and Wales.
roman-britain.o: Julius Caesar raided Britain in 55 and 54 BCE, but conquest began only in 43, when Claudius sent Aulus Plautius with four legions. Camulodunum fell, and over the next forty years the army pushed west and north, overcoming the revolt of Boudica in 60 or 61 and reaching the far north under Agricola, who defeated the Caledonians at Mons Graupius in 83 or 84.
roman-britain.r: Britain was governed by a senatorial legate commanding up to three legions, based at Caerleon, Chester and York. Hadrian's Wall, begun in 122, and briefly the Antonine Wall marked the northern frontier. Severus divided the province in two, and later four provinces formed a diocese. Towns such as Londinium, the main city, grew with fora and baths; villas, wool, grain, lead and tin sustained the economy. Christianity spread from the 3rd century.
roman-britain.e: From the late 3rd century Saxon, Pictish and Irish raids increased, and usurpers such as Carausius and Constantine III drew troops away. By about 410, when Honorius reportedly told the cities to look to their own defence, Roman rule had ended. Successor kingdoms such as the Kingdom of Powys and the Kingdom of Dumnonia arose from its remains.

republic-of-pisa.t: A Tuscan maritime republic that dominated the western Mediterranean in the 12th century and left the Piazza dei Miracoli with its famous leaning tower.
republic-of-pisa.o: Pisan fleets attacked Muslim bases in Sardinia, Sicily and North Africa in the 11th century, and booty from a raid on Palermo in 1063 paid for the cathedral. Consuls governing the city are attested by 1085. Archbishop Daibert led a Pisan fleet in the First Crusade and became the first Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem.
republic-of-pisa.r: Pisa built trading quarters in Acre, Tyre, Constantinople and Alexandria, ruled much of Sardinia and Corsica, and conquered the Balearic Islands briefly in 1113–1115. Loyal to the emperors, it was a Ghibelline stronghold. Its merchants brought back Arabic learning: Leonardo Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe. The cathedral square, with baptistery and bell tower begun in 1173, shows its wealth.
republic-of-pisa.e: Genoa destroyed the Pisan fleet at Meloria in 1284, and the Kingdom of Aragon took Sardinia in 1324. Weakened by faction and the silting of its port, Pisa was sold to the Republic of Florence in 1405 and surrendered after a siege in 1406.

republic-of-brescia.t: A republic proclaimed in Brescia in March 1797 when the city overthrew Venetian rule, one of the blows that hastened the end of Venice.
republic-of-brescia.o: Brescia had been a Venetian mainland city since 1426. On 18 March 1797, a few days after Bergamo, local patriots backed by French troops and Bergamasque volunteers seized power, expelled the Venetian governor and proclaimed the Brescian Republic.
republic-of-brescia.r: The provisional government abolished Venetian institutions, planted liberty trees and raised a national guard. It sent forces to spread the revolt to the Brescian valleys and Lake Garda towns, where peasants loyal to Venice and the Church resisted. It depended on French protection, and its leaders sought union with the Lombard republics.
republic-of-brescia.e: After the fall of the Republic of Venice in May 1797, Brescia was incorporated into the Cisalpine Republic in late 1797.

republic-of-siena-at-montalcino.t: The last stand of the Sienese republic, kept alive in the hill town of Montalcino with French support for four years after Siena fell.
republic-of-siena-at-montalcino.o: When Siena surrendered to imperial and Florentine forces in April 1555, several hundred citizens who refused to submit withdrew to the fortified town of Montalcino, south of the city, and continued the government of the Republic of Siena there under French protection.
republic-of-siena-at-montalcino.r: The exiles kept the republic's magistracies and seal, minted coins and governed Montalcino and a few nearby towns. They depended on French troops and on Piero Strozzi, the Florentine exile who commanded for France in Tuscany. The republic's territory was small, its resources were slight and it lived under the constant threat of the Duchy of Florence.
republic-of-siena-at-montalcino.e: The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis between France and Spain in 1559 withdrew French support, and Montalcino surrendered to Cosimo I de' Medici, joining the future Grand Duchy of Tuscany. The town's people are still nicknamed the last Sienese.

rhode.t: A small Greek colony at Roses on the Catalan coast, linked to Emporion and Massalia, whose silver coins bore a rose.
rhode.o: Ancient writers credited Rhode to settlers from Rhodes, but archaeology shows a Greek settlement founded in the 5th to 4th century BCE, probably by Massalia or nearby Emporion, on the Gulf of Roses in north-east Catalonia.
rhode.r: Rhode was a small Greek trading town with its own pottery workshops. In the 3rd century BCE it minted silver drachms showing a rose, a pun on its name, widely copied in southern Gaul. Excavations in the Ciutadella of Roses have uncovered its houses and streets.
rhode.e: During the north-eastern revolt of 195 BCE Rhode was held against Rome and was captured by Cato. It continued as a small town under Roman rule, later giving its name to Roses.

republic-of-lucca.t: A silk-weaving Tuscan city-republic that kept its independence behind its great walls for over six centuries, until Napoleon.
republic-of-lucca.o: Lucca had been the capital of the march of Tuscany, and a commune of consuls emerged in the late 11th century. In 1160 Duke Welf VI granted the city wide rights, confirming its self-government over the surrounding district.
republic-of-lucca.r: Lucca prospered from silk weaving and banking, and venerated the Volto Santo crucifix. Castruccio Castracani made himself lord from 1316 to 1328 and won a large state, but after his death the city was sold among foreign lords until Emperor Charles IV restored its freedom in 1369. Paolo Guinigi ruled as lord from 1400 to 1430. Afterwards an oligarchy of merchant families governed, building the massive walls of the 16th and 17th centuries.
republic-of-lucca.e: The French occupied Lucca in 1799, and in 1805 Napoleon replaced the republic with the Principality of Lucca and Piombino for his sister Elisa.

republic-of-bologna.t: The city-republic of Europe's oldest university and its forest of towers, which held a captive king for 23 years and later flourished under the Bentivoglio.
republic-of-bologna.o: In 1116 Emperor Henry V granted privileges to the citizens of Bologna, the starting point of the commune. Its law school, traditionally dated to 1088 and associated with the jurist Irnerius, drew students from all over Europe and made the city famous.
republic-of-bologna.r: Bologna was ruled by consuls, then a podestà and popular councils. Noble families built hundreds of defensive towers, including the Asinelli and Garisenda. Guelph Bologna captured King Enzo, son of Frederick II, at Fossalta in 1249 and held him until his death in 1272; the Liber Paradisus of 1256 freed the serfs of its countryside. Nominally under the Papal States, the city was dominated by the Pepoli and then the Bentivoglio families.
republic-of-bologna.e: Pope Julius II marched on Bologna in 1506 and drove out Giovanni II Bentivoglio. The city then passed under direct papal rule, which lasted until 1796, when it briefly became the Bolognese Republic.

republic-of-genoa.t: A maritime republic whose fleets and bankers dominated Mediterranean and Black Sea trade and later financed the Spanish Empire, lasting nearly seven centuries.
republic-of-genoa.o: Genoese citizens formed a sworn association, the compagna communis, around 1099, as fleets returned rich from the First Crusade under leaders such as Guglielmo Embriaco. The commune won trading privileges in the crusader states and fought Pisa and Muslim powers for the western Mediterranean.
republic-of-genoa.r: Genoa built colonies at Pera beside Constantinople, Caffa in the Crimea and Chios, and destroyed Pisa's fleet at Meloria in 1284. Factions of great families, the Doria, Spinola, Fieschi and Grimaldi, competed for power; from 1339 doges such as Simone Boccanegra headed the state. The Bank of Saint George, founded in 1407, managed public debt and colonies. Columbus was a Genoese.
republic-of-genoa.e: After losing the War of Chioggia to Venice in 1381, Genoa often fell under French or Milanese rule. Andrea Doria's constitution of 1528 created an aristocratic republic allied to Habsburg Spain, which Genoese bankers financed. Genoa sold Corsica to France in 1768 and became the Ligurian Republic in 1797.

republic-of-siena.t: Florence's great Tuscan rival, a banking and wool republic whose Palazzo Pubblico frescoes picture the ideals of good government.
republic-of-siena.o: Siena's citizens took power from their bishop in the early 12th century, and consuls are recorded by 1125. Lying on the Via Francigena pilgrim road, the commune prospered from banking and trade and expanded its territory across southern Tuscany.
republic-of-siena.r: Siena was generally Ghibelline and crushed Florence at Montaperti in 1260 under leaders such as Provenzan Salvani. From 1287 to 1355 the merchant government of the Nine built the Palazzo Pubblico, where Ambrogio Lorenzetti painted his Allegory of Good and Bad Government in 1338–1339. Duccio and Simone Martini made the city a centre of painting. The Black Death of 1348 halted its growth; the Monte dei Paschi bank dates from 1472.
republic-of-siena.e: After a period of rule by Pandolfo Petrucci, Siena rebelled against a Spanish garrison in 1552. Imperial and Florentine troops besieged it until it surrendered in April 1555. Exiles continued as the Republic of Siena at Montalcino, and Siena was granted to the Duchy of Florence in 1557.

rani.t: A Slavic people on the island of Rügen whose temple of Svantevit at Arkona was the last great pagan sanctuary on the Baltic until the Danes destroyed it.
rani.o: The Rani were West Slavic settlers of the island of Rügen and nearby coast from around the 8th or 9th century. Their island position and the prestige of their sanctuary gave them influence over neighbouring Slavic peoples, and they are mentioned in German and Danish chronicles from the 10th century.
rani.r: The Rani were ruled by princes, but Saxo Grammaticus and Helmold of Bosau describe the high priest of Arkona as the real power. The temple of the four-faced god Svantevit stood on a cliff at Cape Arkona, receiving tribute from other Slavs and keeping a sacred white horse for divination. The Rani raided Danish coasts and traded across the Baltic.
rani.e: In 1168 King Valdemar I of Denmark and Bishop Absalon captured Arkona and destroyed the idol of Svantevit. Prince Jaromar I accepted Christianity and Danish overlordship, founding the Principality of Rügen, which lasted until its absorption into the Duchy of Pomerania in 1325.

republic-of-cospaia.t: A tiny Umbrian republic born of a surveying error in 1440 that lived for nearly four centuries largely on tax-free tobacco.
republic-of-cospaia.o: In 1440 Pope Eugene IV sold Borgo Sansepolcro to the Republic of Florence. The new border was set along a stream, but two streams had the same name, and a strip of land about two kilometres long between them was left out of both states. Its few hundred inhabitants declared themselves independent.
republic-of-cospaia.r: Cospaia had no army, no prisons and no written constitution; a council of elders and heads of families settled affairs in the church. Its motto, Perpetua et firma libertas, was carved over the church door. From the 16th century the villagers grew tobacco, which escaped the monopolies and taxes of the Papal States and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, and the hamlet became a centre for smuggling.
republic-of-cospaia.e: In 1826 the Papal States and Tuscany agreed to divide the territory. The inhabitants accepted in return for a silver coin each and the right to keep growing tobacco.

republic-of-alba.t: A republic proclaimed for a few days in the Piedmontese town of Alba in 1796, the first Jacobin republic on Italian soil.
republic-of-alba.o: As Napoleon's army drove back the Piedmontese troops of the Kingdom of Sardinia in April 1796, local Jacobins led by Ignazio Bonafous and the exiled publicist Giovanni Antonio Ranza entered Alba and proclaimed a republic, hoping for French support for a revolution in Piedmont.
republic-of-alba.r: The republic planted a liberty tree and issued proclamations calling on the Piedmontese to rise, but it had no real institutions and relied on the presence of French troops. Its leaders hoped to spread the revolution to other towns of southern Piedmont.
republic-of-alba.e: Napoleon preferred to make peace with the king. The Armistice of Cherasco, signed on 28 April 1796, returned Alba to the Kingdom of Sardinia, and the republic disappeared after only a few days.

ruteni.t: Gallic people of the Rouergue whose land later produced the red samian pottery of La Graufesenque, sold across the Roman world.
ruteni.o: The Ruteni lived in the modern Aveyron, around Segodunum (Rodez). After 121 BCE part of their territory was annexed to the Roman Province, so that Caesar distinguishes the Ruteni provinciales from the independent Ruteni.
ruteni.r: They were clients of the Arverni. Their land held silver mines, and they struck their own coins.
ruteni.e: The independent Ruteni joined Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. Under Rome Segodunum became Rodez, and the workshops of La Graufesenque near Millau made millions of red-gloss pots exported as far as India. The medieval Rouergue kept their name.

republic-of-liege.t: The short-lived revolutionary government of Liège, which drove out its prince-bishop in 1789 in a 'happy revolution' inspired by events in Paris.
republic-of-liege.o: Resentment against the authoritarian prince-bishop Constantin-François de Hoensbroeck had grown among Liège's burghers and Enlightenment-minded elites. On 18 August 1789, weeks after the fall of the Bastille, citizens seized the town hall and installed new mayors; the prince-bishop fled, and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège came under patriot control.
republic-of-liege.r: The patriots, led by Jacques-Joseph Fabry and Jean-Rémy de Chestret, governed through a revived city council and the estates, proclaimed the rights of citizens and sought support from Prussia, whose troops briefly occupied the city. The revolution was largely bloodless and called the 'happy revolution', though divisions grew between moderates and radicals.
republic-of-liege.e: After Prussia withdrew, Austrian troops of the Holy Roman Empire restored the prince-bishop in January 1791. His return was brief: French armies arrived in 1792 and again in 1794, and Liège was annexed to France in 1795.

regional-defence-council-of-aragon.t: An anarchist-led regional government in eastern Aragon during the Spanish Civil War, known for its sweeping rural collectives.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.o: In the summer of 1936 anarchist militia columns from Catalonia advanced into eastern Aragon, where collectives sprang up in hundreds of villages. In October 1936 the CNT created the Regional Defence Council of Aragon, first at Fraga and then at Caspe, under Joaquín Ascaso.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.r: The council organised the collectivisation of land and trade, in some villages abolishing money, and coordinated supplies for the Aragon front. It was later broadened to include other Republican parties and was recognised by Largo Caballero's government in December 1936, though Communists and Republicans criticised it.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.e: After the May Days of 1937 weakened the anarchists, the Negrín government dissolved the council in August 1937. Enrique Líster's troops arrested its leaders and broke up many collectives. Aragon was overrun by Franco in 1938.

roman-republic-1849.t: The republic proclaimed in Rome in 1849 and led by Mazzini, whose defence by Garibaldi against French troops became a legend of Italian unification.
roman-republic-1849.o: After the murder of Pope Pius IX's minister Pellegrino Rossi in November 1848, the pope fled to Gaeta in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. An elected Constituent Assembly met in Rome and on 9 February 1849 abolished the temporal power of the Papal States and proclaimed a republic.
roman-republic-1849.r: A triumvirate of Giuseppe Mazzini, Aurelio Saffi and Carlo Armellini governed. The republic abolished the death penalty, introduced religious freedom and drafted a democratic constitution, promulgated on 3 July 1849. Giuseppe Garibaldi led volunteers in defence of the city, notably on the Janiculum hill.
roman-republic-1849.e: Louis-Napoleon's France sent an army under General Oudinot, which besieged Rome from June and entered the city in early July 1849. Garibaldi retreated with his volunteers, and papal rule was restored under French protection.

republic-of-crema.t: A brief Jacobin republic proclaimed in Crema in March 1797, when the town broke from Venice in the last weeks of the Serenissima.
republic-of-crema.o: Crema, a Lombard town between Milan and Cremona, had belonged to the Republic of Venice since 1449. On 28 March 1797, following the revolts of Bergamo and Brescia and with French troops present, local patriots deposed the Venetian governor and proclaimed the Cremasque Republic.
republic-of-crema.r: The republic was a provisional government of local notables and Jacobins under French protection. It abolished Venetian institutions and noble privileges, set up committees on the French model and looked to union with the new Lombard republics. Little is known of its brief administration.
republic-of-crema.e: After the fall of Venice in May 1797, Crema was absorbed into the Cisalpine Republic later that year, ending its separate existence.

republic-of-san-marino.t: Tiny republic on Monte Titano that claims to be the oldest surviving sovereign state and republic in the world, traditionally founded in 301.
republic-of-san-marino.o: Tradition holds that Saint Marinus, a Christian stonemason from the island of Rab in Dalmatia, founded a monastic community on Monte Titano on 3 September 301 to escape persecution under Diocletian. A self-governing community around the monastery and fortress is documented from the early Middle Ages, with an assembly of household heads, the Arengo.
republic-of-san-marino.r: San Marino has been governed since at least the 13th century by two Captains Regent elected every six months, with a Great and General Council as legislature. Its statutes of 1600 served as a written constitution. It kept its independence through its mountain position, alliances with the Montefeltro and recognition by the Papacy in 1631. Catholicism and Italian are dominant; the economy today rests on tourism, banking and stamps.
republic-of-san-marino.e: San Marino survived the occupation by Cardinal Alberoni in 1739–40, declined Napoleon's offer of more territory in 1797, sheltered Garibaldi in 1849 and was left independent at Italian unification. It joined the Council of Europe in 1988 and the United Nations in 1992.

republic-of-sassari.t: A self-governing Sardinian city-republic that rose from the ruins of the Judicate of Logudoro and wrote its laws partly in Sardinian.
republic-of-sassari.o: After the death of Adelasia ended the Judicate of Logudoro in 1259, the growing town of Sassari took control of its own affairs and part of the surrounding territory. From 1272 it governed itself as a commune under Pisan influence, before allying with the Republic of Genoa in 1294.
republic-of-sassari.r: The free commune was led by a podestà sent from Genoa and local councils. Its statutes of 1316, the Statuti Sassaresi, survive in Latin and Sardinian versions and regulated trade, farming and justice. Sassari lived from grain, livestock and trade through Porto Torres.
republic-of-sassari.e: In 1323 Sassari submitted to the Infante Alfonso of the Kingdom of Aragon at the start of the Aragonese conquest, becoming part of the new Kingdom of Sardinia. It revolted several times in the following years.

republic-of-saint-titus.t: Rebel republic proclaimed by Venetian colonists in Crete in 1363, which briefly united Latin and Greek Cretans against Venice.
republic-of-saint-titus.o: In 1363 Venice demanded a new tax from the feudal settlers of Venetian Crete to pay for repairs to the harbour of Candia. The colonists, already resentful at being excluded from power in Venice, rebelled under leaders including Marco Gradenigo and Tito Venier, imprisoned the Venetian duke and proclaimed independence under Saint Titus, patron of Crete.
republic-of-saint-titus.r: The rebels formed a government in Candia led by a governor and councillors. To win Greek support they made concessions to the Orthodox church and drew in Greek nobles such as the Kallergis family. Their republic lacked outside allies: the pope and other powers backed Venice.
republic-of-saint-titus.e: Venice sent a mercenary army under Luchino dal Verme, which retook Candia in May 1364. Leaders were executed and Saint Mark's banner restored, though Greek rebels led by the Kallergis brothers fought on until 1367.
